$comment: Sentences that must read identically wherever they appear.
This is a CHECK, not a generator. There is no build step in this repository —
netlify.toml is `publish = "."` — so a generator would have to rewrite prose
inside two HTML files at commit time. That is a mechanism to trust. A check is a
mechanism to verify, and divergence is the failure that actually matters.
Each entry is keyed by the value of a data-shared-copy attribute. Every element
carrying that attribute, in any HTML file, must contain every phrase listed.
A page that carries the attribute and drops a phrase fails the build; so does a
key that no page claims at all.

completeness.why: The supervisor page and the homepage register row must state the completeness problem in the same words. They are read by the same person in one sitting, and two phrasings of one unsolved problem reads as two different problems. NARROWED 24 August 2026, on a ruling: /supervisors section 04 is the canonical home and stays as it is; the homepage row is compressed to three sentences and links to it. The two sentences both pages still state stay pinned. "The cryptography for transparency logs is solved." left the pin because the compressed row no longer carries it; it remains on /supervisors, unpinned. This narrows the control, and the narrowing is recorded here rather than in a commit message.
completeness.movedOn: 2026-08-24. The homepage row compressed; the pin narrowed from three phrases to the two both pages state.
phrases: A firm can hand over a hundred clean determinations and withhold the hundred-and-first, and all hundred verify.
who runs the log, who is obliged to publish to it, what a gap in it legally means, and how a firm demonstrates completeness without exposing commercially sensitive volume.

offline-scope.why: ENUMERATION ENTRY, not a phrase check. Every place the site claims verification needs nothing from us is tagged data-shared-copy="offline-scope", so there is one place that knows where the claim lives. The claim is currently unscoped on purpose. CORRECTED 2026-08-20: this said the gap it would be scoped for is `refusalPayload` not being exported. THAT PREMISE WAS FALSE AND HAD BEEN FOR RELEASES. `refusalPayload`, `signableFromRefusal`, `REFUSAL_PAYLOAD_TYPE` and `REFUSAL_PAYLOAD_TYPE_V2` are all exported at the version npm's `latest` serves, and the refusal route on /check was built against them the day this was corrected. So the site documented an absence that had ended, and the route nobody wrote was never blocked by the thing this rationale said was blocking it. The failure is not the false sentence: it is that a rationale describing somebody else's package was written once and never re-checked against it, the same shape as a claim about a hosted deployment going stale with no commit here to trigger a review. If a real scope is ever needed, adding one phrase to `phrases` below scopes every instance at once and CI reports the ones not updated.
claimPatterns: no Observer Protocol API in the path
makes no network call at all
No Observer Protocol infrastructure in the verification path
offline-scope.claimPatternsAreRegex: Case-insensitive regexes, matched by check-shared-copy.mjs. Written from the site's own examples rather than from one remembered sentence: the claim is spelled 'call back to us' on index.html and 'callback to Observer' on docs.html, and a literal lower-case list saw neither the capitalised heading nor the Observer variant. Four assertions were invisible to this block on 2026-08-09 for exactly that reason. When you add a home for the claim, add its WORDING here, not just its file.
offline-scope.theWordOfflineWasMissingEntirely: 2026-08-09, second pass. ZERO of the eighteen patterns above contained the word 'offline' — the plainest way the site says this, and the way the org's own GitHub description says it ('verifiable offline by anyone'). Nine untagged instances were live, including a capability pill on index.html, the thesis sentence on docs.html ('Offline verification is not an SDK detail. It is the protocol's central affordance'), and 'The offline path is the claim' on verify.html. The eighteen patterns were each written from a sentence somebody had READ; the vocabulary nobody happened to read in the hour the list was written was simply absent, and the enumeration reported complete throughout. A pattern list records where its author has been. The five patterns added here are claim-shaped on purpose: `offline.didDocumentPath` is a config key appearing nine times and matching it would force allowlist rows for non-claims, which is the failure the allowlist exists to avoid.
offline-scope.theBrowserWasANewVocabulary: 2026-08-17. /check.html is the first surface where the claim is about the VISITOR'S machine rather than about a reader running npm, and it spells it three ways this list had never seen: 'nothing you paste leaves this browser', 'makes no network request', 'checked in your browser'. Zero of the twenty-three patterns matched any of them, so the page would have been a fourth untagged home for the estate's central claim on the day it shipped. Same failure as the word 'offline' being absent from all eighteen patterns on 2026-08-09, and found the same way: by writing the prose and then asking what would have caught it. One of the three instances is inside the page's <script>, in a refusal reason shown to a visitor whose decider is a did:web. The script element is tagged rather than reworded, because an assertion a visitor reads is an assertion whether or not it is in prose.
offline-scope.claimPatternNote: Any occurrence of these in an HTML file MUST sit inside an element tagged data-shared-copy="offline-scope". That is what makes a tenth instance a build failure rather than a discovery. Add the tag, or add the file to mustAppearIn if it is a new home for the claim. Some tagged instances REFER to the claim rather than asserting it (docs.html's resolution-hosting rationale is one). They are tagged anyway: the enumeration's job is to know everywhere the phrase appears, and a human scoping the claim decides per instance.

verifiable-set.why:
PHRASE CHECK, not an enumeration. The list of what a counterparty can verify without us is the estate's central claim and it MOVES: refusal records joined it at engine rc.9, and determinations, resolutions, instructions and releases are named work rather than permanent exclusions. When one of them lands, every sentence stating the set goes stale on the same day, and a stale version of this sentence UNDERSTATES what we can prove, which is the failure nobody reports because it reads as caution.

MEASURED 2026-08-10, and it is why this key exists rather than relying on offline-scope: with the set sentence WIDENED to include releases, NARROWED to "delegation credentials only", and DELETED outright, check-shared-copy exited 0 on all three. offline-scope carries an empty `phrases` array by design: it knows WHERE the claim lives, not WHAT it says. Deleting the sentence passed because index.html carries other offline-scope blocks, so mustAppearIn was still satisfied.

WHAT THIS CATCHES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. `phrases` is satisfied by ANY tagged block in the file, so this fails when a file stops stating the set anywhere, and it does NOT fail when one of two statements in the same file drifts while the other stays correct. index.html states the set twice, so that gap is real there; verify.html states it once, so it is exact. Widening the list breaks the pinned string at the conjunction, which is the direction that matters most.
verifiable-set.movedOn: 2026-08-17. The set widened to include decision attestations, and the pinned run moved with it. This is the event the paragraph above anticipated, so the note it predicted is written here rather than in a commit message. WHAT WAS MEASURED, against the version npm's latest tag serves: verify-samples/ppp-determination-refused-outcome.json is a published op.decision.attestation and verify-published-credentials.mjs returns allow=true on it through verifyDecisionAttestation, which every published tarball from rc.8 to rc.19 exports. The record stores the wire document as base64 with a documentHash, and sha256 over those bytes reproduces it, so the verifier's input is rebuildable from the record alone. The word 'determinations' LEFT the excluded list and 'policy evaluation credentials' took its place, because the old wording named one artifact and excluded two: a PolicyEvaluationCredential still has no verifier path at any published version, a decision attestation has had one throughout, and results/signed-record-coverage.json was already calling the second kind 'determination' while index.html was excluding it under the same word.
phrases: delegation credentials, refusal records, lapse records and decision attestations
verifiable-set.claimPatternNote: Added 2026-08-17, on the corollary in CONVENTIONS 8: the wording you write to correct a claim is a new instance of that claim, and until now this key had `phrases` but no matcher, so a FOURTH statement of the set on an untagged page would not have failed anything. `phrases` catches a tagged block that drifts; these catch a block nobody tagged. Both halves of the set are matched, the positive run and the excluded run, because the defect this key exists for is one of the two moving without the other.

verifiable-set-excluded.why: The negative half, kept as its own key because it is stated on index.html and not on verify.html, and `phrases` applies to every file in a key's mustAppearIn. Splitting is the alternative to weakening the positive key's coverage to the intersection of both pages. The conjunction is deliberately excluded from the pinned string: index.html says "instructions or releases" in one place and "instructions and releases" in the other, and pinning the shorter run keeps both sites honest without pinning a comma.
verifiable-set-excluded.movedOn: 2026-08-17. Was "determinations, resolutions, instructions". A decision attestation is a determination and it verifies against the published engine, so keeping the word here excluded an artifact the estate can prove. A PolicyEvaluationCredential is also a determination and still has no verifier path anywhere, so the exclusion is real and now names the artifact it is true of. If a verifier for the type is ever published, this string moves again and index.html is the only file it lives in.

crossrail-budget-scope.why: ENUMERATION ENTRY, not a phrase check. Same shape as offline-scope and created for the same reason one surface out. The cross-rail budget claim was corrected so thoroughly that crossrail.html was rewritten around 'The budget is a design. The ceiling is a control.', and the correction was placed above the transcript per CONVENTIONS 2d. It was never applied to crossrail.html's own <meta name="description"> or og:description, which asserted 'one cross-rail budget' unqualified until 2026-08-09. A META DESCRIPTION IS THE ONE SURFACE WHERE POSITION CANNOT HELP: it travels alone into a search result and a social card, with no page under it for a correction to sit on, so every positional rule in CONVENTIONS 2c/2d/11 is structurally unavailable there. The claim is enumerated rather than banned because the budget is real, it is simply not adversarially binding: it is an agent-owned local append-only file the agent can truncate, shared only by adapters co-located in one process, and it has never run in production.
crossrail-budget-scope.claimPatternNote: Any occurrence in an HTML file MUST sit inside an element tagged data-shared-copy="crossrail-budget-scope". Instances that STATE the limit are tagged too, not just instances that assert the capability: the enumeration's job is to know everywhere the subject appears so one edit can scope all of them, and a correction is exactly the text that must be revisited when the mechanism changes. If the budget ever becomes signed, or cross-process, or non-resettable, this list is where to find every sentence that has to move.

deprecated-sdk.why: A page may name a deprecated package — there is no replacement for the register/attest flows, so instructing it is sometimes correct. What is never correct is instructing it SILENTLY. On 2026-08-09 four pages disclosed the deprecation and four did not, and the four that did not included the integration guide end to end, under the heading 'Ship chargeback prevention today'. This is not a $forbidden stem: the package name is allowed, the omission is not. Verified at the registry, not from our own copy: npm carries the deprecation notice on the package, and PyPI's newest observer-protocol is 0.2.0 from 2026-04-30.
deprecated-sdk.note: mustAlsoContain is matched case-insensitively anywhere in the same FILE, not the same element: a page-level notice covers every mention on that page, which is how the four disclosing pages already do it. Stem, not phrase — 'deprecat' catches deprecated/deprecation/deprecates, because the last three vocabulary misses on this site were all a matcher that knew one spelling of its subject.

reputation-model.why: Reputation was ruled off this site entirely. It was cleared three times and was wrong three times, because each search was shaped like the previous fix: the phrase, then the subject, then the subject as previously written. 'trust scoring' does not contain 'trust score' — the stem diverges at scor|e versus scor|ing. This forbids the STEM, so a gerund, a bare noun, or a number with a label cannot reappear unnoticed.

allow.why: The line reads 'Refusal at the policy layer, NOT the trust score.' It is the correct usage and the best sentence in the estate on the distinction.
Alt text describes what the screenshot shows, and the screenshot shows an AT-ARS score. Editing it would make the alt text lie about the image.
Inside the comment recording that the score gate was removed and must not be replaced.
The 410 page explains what the retired quickstarts described. Naming the retired thing is the point.

Dated paper, 17 March 2026. Annotated rather than rewritten. The editor's note now covers BOTH retired claims: the 'verified transactions' predicate AND the reputation model. It covered only the first until 2026-08-09, so this exemption was granted for an annotation that did not mention the stem it exempts. A note that exists makes a note that is incomplete harder to see.

An allowlist reason that describes a control which does not exist is indistinguishable from a real exception. The note now exists and names the reputation model specifically.

reputation-model.stemNote: Stems match at a WORD BOUNDARY, not as substrings: 'discord' contains 'scor' and is not a reputation claim. Anchoring removed that false positive rather than allowlisting it.
